network.overall_strategy: The supplied literature does not establish a confirmed end-to-end prebiotic synthesis of free glutamine. This connected network therefore distinguishes experimentally supported precursor chemistry from explicitly speculative glutamine-forming reactions. Exactly ten candidate pathways are enumerated: four glutamate-supply branches, each combined with two proposed activation strategies, and two alternative selective-hydrolysis sequences from the glutamine/glutamate dinitrile precursor. These are ten distinct reaction sequences, not ten demonstrated syntheses. Small organic molecules and specified redox or activation reagents are boundary feedstocks; their simultaneous geochemical availability is not assumed. Final glutamine formation is restricted to cool, UV-shielded waters, with competing hydrolysis and pyroglutamate formation represented explicitly. No molecular oxygen, enzymes, ATP, or stereoselectivity is assumed. Neutral acid/base formulas provide bookkeeping representations of pH-dependent species. For molecules formed in multiple settings, environment_formed gives one representative setting; individual reaction environments are authoritative.

reactions.name: Copper-mediated oxidative coupling to cyanoacetylene
agents: Copper-chloride coordination medium in concentrated chloride brine

conditions.temperature: Approximately ambient; proposed field window 300-310 K
conditions.catalyst: Copper-chloride coupling system; Cu(II) is additionally consumed as oxidant
conditions.other: Sequential reagent delivery, excess HCN for release from copper-bound intermediates, no O2. Copper ions in the graph represent their chloride-complexed pools; chloride is a spectator ligand.

reactions.mechanism: Oxidative coupling of acetylene with cyanide-derived carbon produces cyanoacetylene while Cu(II) accepts reducing equivalents and becomes Cu(I).
reactions.reasoning: Cyanoacetylene production by this chemistry is experimentally supported by Patel et al. (2015). The graph explicitly consumes Cu(II), rather than assuming oxygen-dependent catalytic regeneration. Its availability on an anoxic surface remains a substantial local geochemical requirement; no regeneration mechanism is asserted here.

reactions.name: Hydrocyanation of cyanoacetylene to maleonitrile

conditions.other: Neutral to mildly alkaline cyanide-containing water. Maleonitrile is one branch of a product mixture, not an exclusive product.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide addition across the activated carbon-carbon triple bond followed by proton transfer gives an unsaturated dinitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) report maleonitrile formation in the cyanoacetylene/HCN network. Competing cyanohydrin and aminonitrile products limit selectivity. Only the chemically relevant maleonitrile branch is expanded toward glutamine.

reactions.name: Sulfide-driven photoreduction of maleonitrile

conditions.other: UV irradiation, with 254 nm used in the cited laboratory framework; dissolved H2S/HS− supplies reducing equivalents. Maleonitrile/fumaronitrile photoisomerization can accompany reduction.

reactions.mechanism: Photogenerated reducing equivalents from sulfide saturate the dinitrile alkene.
reactions.reasoning: The succinonitrile-forming transformation is supported by Patel et al. (2015). S8 is a balanced terminal representation of oxidized sulfur, not a claim that the experiment exclusively produced cyclooctasulfur; polysulfides may intervene. Natural UV spectra and sufficient dissolved sulfide remain environmental uncertainties (Ranjan et al., 2018).

reactions.name: Selective photoreduction of one succinonitrile nitrile

conditions.other: Sequential UV/sulfide exposure with controlled residence time. Sulfur products are represented by the same terminal S8 bookkeeping convention as rxn_003.

reactions.mechanism: Reduction of one nitrile to an imine followed by hydrolysis gives 3-cyanopropanal and ammonia while retaining the second nitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) experimentally obtained the semialdehyde from succinonitrile. This unusually useful selectivity supports retaining the nitrile route. It does not establish selective hydrolysis of the later aminodinitrile to glutamine.

reactions.name: Cyanohydrin formation from 3-cyanopropanal

conditions.other: Controlled HCN/cyanide addition near neutral pH after the photoreduction stage.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide adds to the aldehyde carbonyl, followed by protonation of the alkoxide.
reactions.reasoning: This cyanohydrin is part of the experimentally demonstrated precursor sequence in Patel et al. (2015). Sequential processing avoids assuming that aldehyde formation, cyanohydrin formation, and subsequent amination are compatible in a single uncontrolled mixture.

reactions.name: Strecker conversion of the cyanohydrin to aminodinitrile

conditions.other: Ammonia supplied after cyanohydrin formation; sufficient total ammonia is required. No enantioselection is assumed.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanohydrin equilibration, imine formation with ammonia, and cyanide capture produce the alpha-aminonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) report approximately 70% aminodinitrile yield over the cyanohydrin/amination sequence from the semialdehyde. That yield applies to 2-aminopentanedinitrile, not glutamine. The study did not demonstrate its conversion into free glutamine.

reactions.name: Complete aminodinitrile hydrolysis to glutamate

conditions.other: Acidic geothermal water, approximately pH 1-2, with residence time to be determined. This is a proposed environmental window, not a reported protocol for this substrate. Cool and neutralize before glutamine-forming steps.

reactions.mechanism: Both nitriles undergo hydration to amides and subsequent hydrolysis to carboxylic acids; the alpha-amino group is retained in the desired branch.
reactions.reasoning: Complete nitrile hydrolysis is conventional chemistry, but the supplied Patel et al. (2015) study stops at the aminodinitrile. Its execution and yield in this proposed geothermal setting are therefore unvalidated. Harsh hydrolysis cannot preserve glutamine and may also promote cyclization or other degradation.

reactions.name: Hydrogen-driven reductive aldol assembly of alpha-ketoglutarate

conditions.other: Near-neutral water at a gas-retaining mineral interface, not an open atmospheric-pressure pool. Glyoxylate and pyruvate are supplied feedstocks. Ammonia can be withheld when alpha-ketoglutarate is to be routed to a different amination module.

reactions.mechanism: Net carbon-carbon assembly through aldol chemistry and hydrogen-dependent reduction produces the C5 ketoacid; this node summarizes a multistep reductive-aldol transformation.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) support H2/Ni-mediated reductive-aldol chemistry supplying alpha-ketoglutarate alongside amino-acid formation. The compressed net reaction does not assert a unique elementary mechanism or overall yield. Concentrated ketoacid feedstocks and a sustained pressurized H2 microenvironment remain supply constraints.

reactions.name: Nickel-catalyzed reductive amination of alpha-ketoglutarate

conditions.other: Anoxic water, approximately pH 7-8, with ammonium/ammonia supplied. The cited work explored millimolar to submolar nitrogen-source concentrations; no universal optimum is assumed.

reactions.mechanism: The keto group forms an imine or related nitrogen-containing intermediate with ammonia, which is hydrogenated on nickel to glutamate.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) directly support mild H2/Ni reductive amination of alpha-ketoglutarate. Nickel is selected for demonstrated hydrogen activation rather than generic mineral adsorption. Glutamate formation is supported; subsequent gamma-amidation is not. Alpha-ketoglutarate is not universally the fastest aminating ketoacid (Mayer and Moran, 2022).

reactions.name: Iron-coupled hydroxylamine conversion of alpha-ketoglutarate to glutamate
agents: Fe(0), explicitly consumed as a reducing agent

conditions.other: Anoxic iron-containing water with hydroxylamine. Exact pH and residence time must be taken from the experimental protocol rather than inferred from the supplied summary. H+ is redox bookkeeping, not a prescription for concentrated acid. Cool before amidation.

reactions.mechanism: Oxime formation is followed by iron-coupled reduction and nitrogen-oxygen bond cleavage. Fe(II) represents oxidation of the metallic reductant; actual surface phases may be more complex.
reactions.reasoning: Muchowska, Varma and Moran (2019) support amino-acid formation, including glutamate, in iron/hydroxylamine chemistry near 70 degrees Celsius. This is chemically distinct from NH3/H2 reductive amination. The availability of hydroxylamine at useful concentrations is a major geochemical limitation, and the displayed equation is a balanced net redox representation rather than a resolved surface mechanism.

reactions.name: Aluminium-assisted transamination from glycine
agents: Dissolved Al(III) supplied by potassium aluminium sulfate

conditions.other: Approximately pH 5; reported example uses 350 mM glycine, 1.2 equivalents alpha-ketoglutarate, 0.1 equivalent alum, and 4 hours. Cool and separate from the hot transamination stage before attempting glutamine formation.

reactions.mechanism: Metal-assisted imine chemistry transfers the glycine amino group to alpha-ketoglutarate, producing glutamate and glyoxylate.
reactions.reasoning: The supplied account of Stubbs et al. (2020) reports approximately 44% glutamate under these conditions. Aluminium is included for the demonstrated transamination chemistry, not as an unspecified mineral template. High reactant concentrations and a suitable local aluminium source limit geochemical generality.

reactions.name: Hypothetical gamma-carboxyl activation by acetyl phosphate

conditions.other: UV-shielded water at approximately pH 6-7; fresh acetyl phosphate is an externally supplied activation reagent. No effective concentration, rate, or selectivity has been demonstrated.

reactions.mechanism: Hypothesized phosphoryl transfer to glutamate's gamma-carboxylate produces an acyl phosphate and acetate.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative and a principal bottleneck. The supplied report proposes acyl-phosphate activation but provides no demonstration of this reaction. Biological gamma-carboxyl activation is only an analogy (Curnow et al., 1997; Oshikane et al., 2006), not evidence that acetyl phosphate selectively activates free glutamate. Competing acetylation, alpha-carboxyl activation, hydrolysis, and cyclization may dominate.

reactions.name: Hypothetical ammonolysis of gamma-glutamyl phosphate

conditions.other: Approximately pH 6-7.5, UV-shielded, with a high local ammonium/ammonia activity and immediate product analysis. The small unprotonated NH3 fraction at this pH may severely limit reaction rate.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia attacks the activated gamma-carbonyl and displaces phosphate, forming the side-chain amide.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative as an abiotic glutamine-forming step. Activated gamma-carboxyl chemistry is biologically precedented, but the cited enzyme/tRNA studies do not establish uncatalyzed ammonolysis of free gamma-glutamyl phosphate (Curnow et al., 1997; Oshikane et al., 2006). Hydrolysis and intramolecular lactamization must be measured against glutamine production. No glutamine yield is assigned.

reactions.name: Hypothetical cyanamide-mediated gamma-amidation of glutamate

conditions.other: Concentrated, UV-shielded water at approximately pH 6-7. Cyanamide is a consumed condensing reagent, not a catalyst. Its useful concentration and activation rate are unknown; heating or exhaustive drying is not assumed.

reactions.mechanism: A proposed cyanamide-derived carboxyl-activation pathway is followed by ammonia capture; urea is the balanced spent-reagent product of the desired net condensation.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative. The supplied research lists cyanamide/carbodiimide-type activation as an untested possibility, not a demonstrated glutamine synthesis. Formation of a reactive activating species, gamma-versus-alpha selectivity, and competition with peptides or pyroglutamate are unresolved. Stability measurements justify cool handling but provide no evidence for this amidation reaction (Arii et al., 1999).

reactions.name: Hypothetical alpha-nitrile hydrolysis with retention of the side-chain nitrile

conditions.other: UV-shielded water, approximately pH 6-7.5. These are target-preserving test conditions, not established productive conditions; uncatalyzed hydrolysis may be prohibitively slow.

reactions.mechanism: The alpha-nitrile is hypothesized to hydrate to an amide and then hydrolyze to the alpha-carboxyl group while the remote nitrile remains intact.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative for this substrate and environment. Green et al. (2023) observed preferential alpha-nitrile hydration in related N-formylaminonitriles, including a shorter-chain analogue, but that does not establish complete alpha-hydrolysis of unprotected 2-aminopentanedinitrile. Substrate protection, chain length, pH, and competing cyclic products are material differences.

reactions.name: Hypothetical side-chain nitrile hydration to glutamine

conditions.other: Approximately pH 6-7.5, UV shielding, short residence after product formation. No mineral is assigned because the supplied evidence establishes no suitable selective catalyst.

reactions.mechanism: Hydration of the remaining nitrile stops at the primary amide rather than continuing to glutamate.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative and a decisive bottleneck. Patel et al. (2015) did not perform this conversion, and Green et al. (2023) provide only related-substrate evidence. Productive hydration must outrun both overhydrolysis and glutamine cyclization; no rate, glutamine yield, or viable selectivity window is known.

reactions.name: Hypothetical side-chain-first hydration of the aminodinitrile

conditions.other: Approximately pH 6-7.5 in UV-shielded water. This is a lower-confidence selectivity hypothesis; no effective catalyst or residence time is established.

reactions.mechanism: The remote nitrile is selectively hydrated to the glutamine side-chain amide while the alpha-aminonitrile remains intact.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative. This order is chemically distinguishable from rxn_015, but it is not experimentally supported and may be disfavored by the faster alpha-nitrile hydration seen in related N-formyl substrates (Green et al., 2023). It is included as an explicit competing selectivity hypothesis, not an equally validated alternative.

reactions.name: Hypothetical alpha-aminonitrile hydrolysis preserving the side-chain amide

conditions.other: Approximately pH 6-7.5, UV shielding, and time-resolved analysis without hot or strongly acidic workup. Rate and usable conversion are unknown.

reactions.mechanism: The alpha-nitrile hydrates through an alpha-carboxamide and hydrolyzes to the carboxyl group while the existing gamma-amide survives.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative. The required differential hydrolysis has not been demonstrated for glutaminonitrile in the supplied research. Related aminonitrile chemistry (Green et al., 2023) does not establish preservation of the gamma-amide during complete alpha-hydrolysis. Ordinary exhaustive hydrolysis would instead yield glutamate.

reactions.name: Competing regioselective hydrolysis to isoglutamine

conditions.other: Evaluate during aminodinitrile hydrolysis across approximately pH 6-7.5. Quantify against authentic glutamine and isoglutamine standards.

reactions.mechanism: The alpha-nitrile stops at the amide while the remote nitrile hydrolyzes fully to the acid, producing the constitutional isomer of glutamine.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative competing branch explicitly identified as an unresolved selectivity problem in the supplied report. A mass match alone cannot distinguish this product from glutamine; the tentative tholin assignment of Neish, Somogyi and Smith (2010) therefore does not validate glutamine production. The reaction is not counted as a target pathway.

reactions.name: Glutamine cyclization to pyroglutamate

conditions.other: Approximately pH 5-7.5. For a stability constraint, use k approximately 0.105 day−1 at 310 K and pH 7.2, corresponding to about 10% daily loss and a 6.6-day half-life. This is an empirical overall-loss anchor, not a universally transferable elementary rate constant.

reactions.mechanism: Intramolecular attack of the alpha-amino group on the side-chain amide carbonyl forms the five-membered lactam and releases ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: Glutamine loss and pyroglutamate formation are experimentally supported by Tritsch and Moore (1962) and Arii et al. (1999). Reported apparent activation energies differ, approximately 48 versus 99 kJ/mol; they should not be merged into a single precise high-temperature prediction. This sink must be included when evaluating whether any hypothetical source can produce net accumulation.

reactions.name: Competing glutamine side-chain deamidation

conditions.temperature: 300-370 K; increasingly important under thermal or pH stress
conditions.other: A competing degradation branch, especially outside the final-product stability window. No independent neutral-pH rate is assigned, avoiding double-counting the overall-loss anchor in rxn_020.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolysis of the side-chain amide regenerates glutamate and releases ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: Airaudo, Gayte-Sorbier and Armand (1987) describe glutamine conversion to glutamate during heating, followed under suitable conditions by pyroglutamate formation. Hot or acid-hydrolytic analytical workups can therefore erase glutamine. The relative contributions of this branch and direct cyclization depend on conditions.

reactions.name: Glutamate dehydration to pyroglutamate

conditions.other: Concentrating geothermal waters or extended warm residence. Rates in this proposed field range are not assigned from higher-temperature food or dry-heating measurements.

reactions.mechanism: Intramolecular condensation between the alpha-amino group and gamma-carboxyl group produces the lactam with water loss.
reactions.reasoning: Gayte-Sorbier, Airaudo and Armand (1985) found that heating glutamate gives pyroglutamate rather than glutamine. This supports the competing transformation but not a quantitative rate at every stated field temperature. The branch explains why simple heating or drying is not treated as a valid glutamine synthesis.

reactions.name: Competing cyclization of activated gamma-glutamyl phosphate

conditions.other: Same compartment as rxn_013. Measure lactam formation directly rather than assuming external ammonia captures the activated acyl group.

reactions.mechanism: The alpha-amino group attacks the activated gamma-carbonyl intramolecularly, displacing phosphate and forming pyroglutamate.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative for this prebiotic acyl-phosphate system, but chemically important because activation also enables a favorable five-membered intramolecular acyl substitution. Glutamate and glutamine lactamization are experimentally established (Gayte-Sorbier et al., 1985; Arii et al., 1999); those studies do not provide a measured rate for gamma-glutamyl phosphate.

reactions.name: Competing hydrolysis of gamma-glutamyl phosphate

conditions.other: Approximately pH 6-7.5. Activated-intermediate lifetime must be measured under the same conditions used for ammonolysis.

reactions.mechanism: Water hydrolyzes the mixed carboxylic-phosphoric anhydride, regenerating glutamate and inorganic phosphate.
reactions.reasoning: An expected acyl-phosphate loss reaction, but its rate in the proposed prebiotic system is unmeasured and therefore speculative quantitatively. Biological activated-carboxyl chemistry (Curnow et al., 1997; Oshikane et al., 2006) cannot be used to assume that the free intermediate survives in bulk water. This branch prevents activation from being treated as automatically productive.

pathways.name: Cyanosulfidic precursor, complete hydrolysis, and acyl-phosphate closure
pathways.description: Build the aminodinitrile from HCN and acetylene, hydrolyze to glutamate, then test acetyl-phosphate activation and ammonolysis. Upstream photochemistry is supported; the proposed hydrolysis setting and glutamine-forming closure are unvalidated.

pathways.name: Cyanosulfidic precursor, complete hydrolysis, and cyanamide closure
pathways.description: Use the same experimentally supported aminodinitrile supply, followed by proposed complete hydrolysis and cyanamide-mediated amidation. This differs from P1 in its activating reagent and activation chemistry, not merely in environmental labels.

pathways.name: Hydrogen/nickel ketoacid assembly and amination with acyl-phosphate closure
pathways.description: Assemble alpha-ketoglutarate from glyoxylate and pyruvate, perform NH3/H2 reductive amination over nickel, and test gamma-carboxyl activation and ammonolysis after transfer to a cool, shielded compartment.

pathways.name: Hydrogen/nickel ketoacid assembly and amination with cyanamide closure
pathways.description: Combine the supported H2/Ni glutamate-supply chemistry with the distinct, unvalidated cyanamide condensation hypothesis. No productive glutamine flux is established.

pathways.name: Iron/hydroxylamine amination with acyl-phosphate closure
pathways.description: Supply alpha-ketoglutarate through reductive-aldol chemistry, then use the experimentally motivated iron/hydroxylamine amination branch. Cool the glutamate-containing solution before the speculative phosphate-mediated closure. Hydroxylamine availability is an additional limitation.

pathways.name: Iron/hydroxylamine amination with cyanamide closure
pathways.description: Use hydroxylamine/iron rather than NH3/H2 to install the alpha-amino group, followed by the unvalidated cyanamide-mediated gamma-amidation. The required nitrogen-source supply and terminal selectivity are not established geochemically.

pathways.name: Glycine transamination with acyl-phosphate closure
pathways.description: Generate alpha-ketoglutarate, transfer nitrogen from glycine under the reported aluminium-assisted transamination conditions, then cool before testing gamma-glutamyl phosphate formation and ammonolysis.

pathways.name: Glycine transamination with cyanamide closure
pathways.description: Combine the glycine-to-glutamate amino-group transfer with the alternative cyanamide activation hypothesis. The warm transamination stage is separated from cool final-product handling because glutamine is thermally fragile.

pathways.name: Aminodinitrile alpha-acid-first selective hydrolysis
pathways.description: After cyanosulfidic aminodinitrile synthesis, first obtain the alpha-carboxyl group while retaining the side-chain nitrile, then hydrate that nitrile only to the amide. Both selective hydrolysis stages remain unvalidated under glutamine-preserving conditions.

pathways.name: Aminodinitrile side-chain-amide-first selective hydrolysis
pathways.description: Form glutaminonitrile by hydrating the remote nitrile first, then hydrolyze the alpha-nitrile without destroying the side-chain amide. This is a lower-confidence alternative order because related protected substrates favor alpha-nitrile hydration. Neither stage is an established prebiotic glutamine synthesis.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Patel et al. (2015) support rxn_001–rxn_006, and complete aminodinitrile hydrolysis is chemically plausible. The decisive gap is rxn_012: acetyl phosphate's activation potential does not establish selective formation of gamma-glutamyl phosphate rather than alternative phosphorylation, acylation or hydrolysis products. Ammonolysis in rxn_013 is plausible conditional on that intermediate being available, but competition with cyclization and hydrolysis is unquantified. Conditions for complete nitrile hydrolysis and subsequent delivery into cool amidation water are unspecified.
suggestions: Specify the sequential photochemical and complete-hydrolysis protocols, followed by cooling and pH adjustment with measured substrate recovery.
Demonstrate gamma-glutamyl phosphate formation from glutamate and acetyl phosphate, distinguishing alpha activation and other products.
Measure glutamine formation against rxn_023 and rxn_024 at specified ammonia concentration, temperature and pH.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The precursor sequence aligns with Patel et al. (2015), but rxn_014 remains an unsupported net condensation. Its balanced conversion of cyanamide to urea does not establish an effective activation mechanism or gamma-carboxyl selectivity. Cyanamide-mediated side reactions, alternative carboxyl activation and pyroglutamate formation remain possible. Cool, shielded water helps product persistence but does not demonstrate that amidation proceeds appreciably.
suggestions: Identify the activating intermediate and operating conditions for cyanamide-mediated amidation rather than relying only on the net equation.
Quantify glutamine, isoglutamine, pyroglutamate and other condensation products using authentic standards.
Establish whether the measured formation rate exceeds glutamine loss under the same conditions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Kaur et al. (2024) provide relevant experimental support for hydrogen-driven ketoacid assembly and nickel-catalyzed reductive amination. However, the 'Biochemical' environment label does not specify an abiotic operating environment: hydrogen pressure, nickel phase, loading and solution conditions remain undefined. The pathway still depends on unvalidated gamma-carboxyl activation in rxn_012. Biological gamma-glutamyl phosphate chemistry supports the chemical logic of rxn_013, not the effectiveness of this enzyme-free implementation.
suggestions: Specify nickel catalyst identity, hydrogen confinement and pressure, pH, concentrations and residence times for rxn_008 and rxn_009.
Test the activation/ammonolysis module using the actual precursor reaction mixture, including residual metals and competing solutes.
Measure activation selectivity and ammonia-dependent branching between glutamine, pyroglutamate and hydrolyzed glutamate.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The glutamate-supply module has relevant support from Kaur et al. (2024), but that evidence does not extend to cyanamide-mediated glutamine formation. Rxn_014 provides neither a demonstrated activation mechanism nor evidence that the gamma carboxyl group reacts selectively. At a glutamine-compatible pH, ammonia is predominantly protonated, so the reactive ammonia concentration and amidation kinetics require explicit treatment.
suggestions: Provide operating conditions for the nickel/hydrogen module and characterize its output mixture.
Measure cyanamide-mediated amidation across a defined temperature and pH range, reporting free ammonia rather than only total ammonium.
Test whether gamma amidation occurs before cyanamide consumption, competing condensation or glutamine degradation.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The supplied Muchowska et al. (2019) findings support iron/hydroxylamine conversion of ketoacids to amino acids. Rxn_010 is conservation-consistent with the inferred two Fe atoms and four protons; its actual pH and reducing conditions still need specification. Alpha-ketoglutarate supply also depends on rxn_008 and its hydrogen/catalyst requirements. Neither precursor module validates rxn_012, and the warmer conditions underlying the iron chemistry must be reconciled physically with the proposed cool glutamine-forming stage.
suggestions: Encode the inferred stoichiometry for rxn_010 and specify iron state, hydroxylamine concentration, temperature and pH.
Describe cooling, pH adjustment and handling of residual iron and hydroxylamine before activation.
Demonstrate the complete activation/ammonolysis module with product and competing-loss measurements.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The glutamate-forming chemistry is supported in principle by the supplied hydrogen-driven assembly and iron/hydroxylamine literature. Environmental compatibility remains unverified because operating conditions and transfer treatment are absent. Cyanamide-mediated gamma amidation is the decisive unsupported step; residual hydroxylamine and other nucleophiles could also alter its product distribution. Declaring the terminal reaction hypothetical appropriately reflects the evidence but does not establish target production.
suggestions: Specify both precursor modules and the composition entering the amidation stage.
Test cyanamide activation in the presence of realistic precursor-mixture carryover, including residual hydroxylamine.
Report structurally confirmed glutamine yield and its time-dependent loss rather than relying on mass assignment alone.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The supplied transamination evidence supports glutamate production from alpha-ketoglutarate and glycine under specified concentrated, aluminium-containing, heated conditions. Those conditions are not supplied for rxn_011, and aluminium availability and speciation are not established by the 'Surface' label. Rxn_008 is a separate hydrogen-driven assembly module, not the metal-free glyoxylate assembly discussed elsewhere in the research. The route remains blocked by unvalidated gamma activation and uncertain competition during ammonolysis.
suggestions: Specify the aluminium species, loading, substrate concentrations and temperature underlying rxn_011.
Document cooling and transfer into the final module, including aluminium and glycine carryover.
Test whether residual glycine competes with ammonia for activated glutamate and quantify glutamine versus cyclization products.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Aluminium-assisted transamination provides a plausible glutamate supply when its experimental conditions are reproduced. It does not establish a compatible cyanamide amidation stage. The unspecified fate of excess glycine and aluminium is important because activation in this mixture could produce competing condensations rather than selective glutamine formation. The final transformation lacks direct support in the supplied literature.
suggestions: Provide reaction-specific conditions and citations for the hydrogen-driven assembly and aluminium-assisted transamination steps.
Characterize competing cyanamide reactions with residual glycine and glutamate's alpha amino group.
Demonstrate selective gamma amidation under conditions compatible with glutamine persistence.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is provisionally the strongest candidate because its proposed differential nitrile reactivity has limited experimental analogy, not because of its framework or step count. Patel et al. (2015) support the aminodinitrile precursor. Green et al. (2023) provide evidence concerning faster alpha-nitrile hydration in related N-formyl substrates, but not complete alpha-nitrile hydrolysis with retention of the side-chain nitrile in this unprotected C5 compound. Subsequent selective hydration to glutamine at cool, compatible conditions is also untested; no catalyst, rate or selectivity is specified.
suggestions: Measure hydrolysis of the actual unprotected C5 aminodinitrile, distinguishing alpha-amide formation from complete alpha-carboxyl formation.
Isolate or identify mol_031 and test its side-chain nitrile hydration under explicitly defined mild conditions.
Use time-resolved chromatography with glutamine, isoglutamine and pyroglutamate standards to determine formation and loss rates.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The precursor synthesis is literature-aligned, but the side-chain-first sequence requires two unestablished selectivities. Rxn_017 must hydrate the terminal nitrile while retaining the alpha-aminonitrile; the related N-formyl substrate evidence does not support assuming that ordering. Rxn_018 must then hydrolyze the alpha nitrile completely while preserving the existing side-chain amide. Both transformations are chemically conceivable, but no suitable selective catalyst or compatible operating window is identified.
suggestions: Identify conditions or a catalyst that experimentally favors side-chain-first hydration of mol_015.
Prepare and characterize mol_032, then measure alpha-nitrile hydrolysis against side-chain deamidation and cyclization.
Compare P9 and P10 experimentally on the same substrate rather than inferring selectivity from related protected compounds.

evaluation.network_feedback: NOT APPROVED as a complete glutamine synthesis: overall confidence is below 0.90. The 35-molecule, 24-reaction network is connected, has no isolated subgraphs and consistently references declared molecule IDs. The deterministic check establishes 16 reactions balanced as written, eight balanceable with coefficients and no conservation violations. Explicitly encode the inferred coefficients for rxn_001, rxn_003, rxn_004, rxn_007, rxn_010, rxn_015, rxn_018 and rxn_019. The factors of eight in the sulfur-producing reactions follow naturally from representing elemental sulfur as S8 and are not intrinsically suspicious. Correct the reported formula/InChI discrepancies for mol_006 and mol_023 and the unparseable InChI for mol_033; these are representation defects, not additional conservation failures. In particular, the target formula alone cannot distinguish glutamine from isoglutamine. Literature alignment is strong in acknowledging the absence of a confirmed end-to-end route, separating supported precursor chemistry from hypotheses and including competing losses. However, reaction-specific citations and experimental conditions are not embedded in the reaction records. Every productive pathway still depends on an unvalidated gamma-amidation or selective nitrile-hydrolysis module. Boundary feedstocks are accepted as declared; neither their particular identities nor pathway multiplicity or shared intermediates raises or lowers confidence. Environmental assessment is limited by missing numerical conditions, catalyst phases and loadings, hydrogen pressure, irradiation details, residence times and physically specified transfers. Cooling and UV shielding address persistence but do not establish productive kinetics. Across the competing branches, rxn_019 represents a plausible isoglutamine outcome, not demonstrated regioselectivity; rxn_020 and rxn_021 are credible glutamine-loss processes supported by the stability literature; rxn_023 and rxn_024 are chemically credible losses of activated glutamate. Rxn_022 is plausible under suitable thermal or dehydrating conditions but should not be assigned rapid conversion in cool water without evidence. These sinks lack the kinetic information needed to establish net glutamine accumulation. P9 ranks highest only provisionally: the cited analogue chemistry does not validate its two selective hydrolysis steps. Overall confidence is constrained by the terminal chemistry and missing integrated operating evidence, rather than averaged upward by supported precursor reactions. The network is a useful experimental hypothesis map, not an established viable synthesis of free glutamine.

mol_023 (Ferrous ion): stated formula Fe2+ disagrees with its InChI structure (stated minus InChI: Fe+1, charge 1 vs 2)
mol_033: InChI could not be parsed by RDKit (RDKit could not parse InChI)
